lessons.title: NPS and the Extra Rs 50,000 Under Section 80CCD(1B)

children.text: Once your ₹1.5 lakh bucket is full, most tax saving stops. The National Pension System is the exception. It offers a separate ₹50,000 deduction over and above the 80C limit, plus an employer contribution benefit that still works on the new regime. The price is a long lock-in until 60 and rules on how you take the money out. This lesson untangles all three NPS deductions and the 2025 changes to exit rules.

markDefs.definition: Tier I is the main NPS pension account. It carries the tax deductions and restricts withdrawals until 60. Tier II is an optional, flexible savings account with no deduction for most people.

body.title: Regime Check
body.question: Nisha, a product lead in Gurugram, is on the new regime. She contributes ₹50,000 of her own money to NPS Tier I, and her employer contributes ₹1,20,000 (well within 14% of her salary). How much NPS deduction can she claim?
options: Nothing, NPS deductions are not allowed on the new regime
body.explanation: On the new regime, only the employer's contribution under Section 124(1) and (2) is deductible, up to 14% of salary. Her own ₹50,000 gets no deduction because Section 124(3) is available only on the old regime.

body.caption: Tax saved by a ₹50,000 contribution under Section 124(3), old regime, when the whole amount falls in one slab

body.title: Your Turn: The Combined Saving
body.prompt: Harish, a senior engineer in Bengaluru on the old regime, is in the 30% slab. His 80C bucket is already full at ₹1,50,000. He adds ₹50,000 to NPS Tier I under Section 124(3). What is his total tax saving from 80C and the NPS extra deduction combined, including 4% cess?
body.explanation: Total deductions = ₹1,50,000 + ₹50,000 = ₹2,00,000. At 30% plus 4% cess: ₹2,00,000 × 31.2% = ₹62,400. The NPS contribution alone adds ₹15,600 to what 80C already saved (₹46,800).

children.text: Employer NPS: The New Regime's Best Tax Tool

If your employer offers NPS as part of CTC, you can ask for part of your salary to be paid into NPS instead of your bank account. On the new regime, up to 14% of basic plus DA becomes deductible. Your CTC does not change; you simply restructure it.

body.caption: Arvind, an engineering manager in Hyderabad on the new regime, 30% slab: basic of ₹1,00,000 a month

body.text: Employer contributions to EPF, NPS and superannuation above ₹7.5 lakh a year in total are taxable as a perquisite, along with the returns on the excess. Also remember that money routed to NPS is locked until 60 under the exit rules below. Do not restructure more salary into NPS than you can afford to lose access to.

cards.definition: Permanent Retirement Account Number: your lifelong NPS account number. It stays the same across jobs and cities.
You decide how your money is split across equity (E), corporate bonds (C), government securities (G) and alternative assets (A), within PFRDA limits.
A life-cycle fund that automatically reduces equity and increases debt as you age.
The company that invests your NPS money, such as SBI Pension Funds, HDFC Pension Fund or ICICI Prudential Pension Fund. You can switch managers.
Introduced from 1 October 2025 for non-government subscribers. Pension funds can offer high-risk variants with up to 100% equity, with a 15-year minimum vesting period.
A pension plan bought from a life insurer with part of your corpus at exit. It pays a fixed income for life, and that income is taxable every year.

children.text: Getting Your Money Out: The 2025 Exit Rules

From December 2025, PFRDA relaxed exit rules for non-government subscribers. At 60 (or after 15 years, or on superannuation), you can now take up to 80% of your corpus as a lump sum, down from 60%, and must use at least 20% to buy an annuity, down from 40%.

body.caption: Normal exit rules for non-government NPS subscribers

cells: Withdraw 100% as a lump sum, no annuity required
Take up to ₹6 lakh as lump sum with the rest through systematic withdrawal or annuity, or take up to 80% as lump sum with at least 20% in annuity
Take up to 80% as lump sum; at least 20% must buy an annuity

body.caption: Illustration: ₹50,000 contributed at the start of each year for 25 years, at an assumed 10% a year.

body.title: Exiting with ₹54.09 lakh at 60, taking the maximum lump sum

body.text: PFRDA's rules now let you withdraw 80%, but tax law still exempts only 60% of the corpus. The extra 20% you take as a lump sum is taxable at your slab in the year you receive it, unless the law is amended. Withdrawing all 80% in one year could push a large chunk into the 30% slab. The annuity income is also taxable every year. Plan the exit, do not just take the maximum.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: A non-government NPS subscriber with a corpus above ₹12 lakh at 60 must use at least ___% of it to buy an annuity.
body.explanation: Since December 2025 the minimum annuity is 20%, down from 40%. Up to 80% can be taken as a lump sum, though only 60% of the corpus is tax-free.

body.title: Go Deeper: Early Exit, Partial Withdrawals and NPS Vatsalya

cells: After 3 years in NPS, up to 25% of your own contributions, maximum 4 times, for specified needs such as children's education, marriage, home purchase or critical illness
Premature exit, corpus up to ₹5 lakh
Lump sum within 60% of corpus is tax-free
After at least 5 years; maximum 20% lump sum, at least 80% into annuity
Lump sum tax-free; annuity income taxable

children.text: NPS Vatsalya lets parents open an NPS account for a minor child. Contributions qualify under Section 124(4) on the old regime, but the ₹50,000 limit is shared with your own Section 124(3) contribution, so it is not an additional ₹50,000 on top.

body.title: Scenario: Worth the Lock-In?
body.scenario: Meghna, 38, is a finance manager in Kochi on the old regime, in the 30% slab. Her 80C is full through EPF and PPF. She has ₹50,000 a year spare and is deciding between NPS Tier I and an index fund. Her employer does not offer NPS in CTC. She is not sure she wants money locked until 60, and she has heard that 'NPS forces you to buy an annuity'.
body.prompt: Lay out the trade-off for Meghna. What would tip the decision either way?
body.modelAnswer: The case for NPS: the ₹50,000 under Section 124(3) saves her ₹15,600 a year, so she effectively invests ₹50,000 for a cost of ₹34,400, a 45% boost on day one. Over 22 years to age 60 that head start compounds substantially. With active choice or a high-risk Multiple Scheme Framework variant, she can hold a large equity allocation at very low fund management costs. The case against: the money is locked until 60 apart from limited partial withdrawals after 3 years (25% of her own contributions, specified purposes). Only 60% of the corpus is tax-free on exit, at least 20% must buy an annuity with taxable income, and the rules have changed several times, so they may change again. An index fund offers full liquidity and gains taxed at only 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh a year, but no upfront deduction. What tips it: if she is confident this is genuinely retirement money and she lacks dedicated retirement savings beyond EPF, NPS's ₹15,600 yearly tax saving is hard to ignore. If she wants the option to use the money at 50 for any purpose, the index fund is the cleaner choice. A split is also reasonable. Her worry about the annuity is overstated: it is now a minimum of 20%, not the whole corpus.

body.title: Setting Up NPS for Tax Benefits
steps: Open a Tier I account through eNPS (Protean or KFintech), your bank, or your employer's corporate NPS
On the old regime: contribute ₹50,000 a year to Tier I to claim Section 124(3), ideally monthly
On the new regime: ask HR whether employer NPS at up to 14% of basic can be added to your CTC
Check total employer EPF plus NPS contributions stay under ₹7.5 lakh a year
Choose your pension fund manager and asset allocation, or auto choice if you prefer not to manage it
Download the NPS contribution statement for your tax proof; Tier II contributions do not count
Revisit your exit plan 3 to 5 years before 60, keeping in mind that only 60% of the corpus is tax-free

body.label: eNPS by Protean
body.description: Open an NPS account, make contributions and download statements online.

points: NPS has three deductions: your own contribution within the ₹1.5 lakh Section 123 limit, an extra ₹50,000 under Section 124(3), and the employer contribution under Section 124(1) and (2).
The extra ₹50,000 works only on the old regime and saves up to ₹15,600 a year at the 30% slab.
Employer NPS up to 14% of salary is deductible on the new regime, making it the new regime's most valuable tax lever.
Since December 2025, non-government subscribers can take up to 80% as a lump sum at 60, with at least 20% in an annuity.
Only 60% of the corpus is tax-free on exit; the extra 20% lump sum and all annuity income are taxable.
NPS is genuine retirement money: access before 60 is limited to partial withdrawals and restricted early exit.

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not tax, investment or legal advice. NPS returns are market-linked and not guaranteed; the projection uses an assumed rate. PFRDA regulations and tax treatment of NPS withdrawals have changed recently and may change again. Consult a qualified professional for decisions specific to your situation.
